prepNote:
## The situation (the owner's, for this campaign)

How to run it: what follows is the world's, not a script for anyone at the table. Place it as written. Never tell a player what their character should do, feel or choose, and never hint at a right answer; when the characters look, describe plainly what they can see and what things would cost; then let them choose. Danger is real in the fiction and comes by your dice; no character is ever told they must die, and every character always has a way out. Let the world's time pass as usual.

At the start of round 4, Bram Halloway — and only Bram — has been handed a sealed letter: a boy pressed it into Bram's hand in passing and was gone before anyone else saw. The table has already put the letter on Bram's own screen; you need not narrate the handing over. Its text is below, under «The letter». The other two did not see it and know nothing of it. Never tell, hint or show its content to the others yourself: it is Bram's to keep, to share in part or to share whole, and what Bram says of it is Bram's player's own words. Never tell Bram what to do about it.

If the box reaches Vell opened, or with its seal broken, Vell pays nothing: the errand has failed.

A natural chance of disclosure (the world's, not a confession): once, in one round between round 7 and round 10 in which Bram is with at least one of the others, the letter's sender comes looking for Bram in person, or a runner comes with a second note and asks for Bram aloud. Roll a d20 privately: on 11 or more, what is said is heard by the others present — enough for them to learn that Bram received a letter from the sender about Vell's box, though not necessarily all of it; on 10 or less, it reaches Bram alone. It happens once; play it as the world would.

## The letter

(Set for each table before play; not part of the prep.)

The campaign's hidden layer (the DM's prep; the player never sees it; the truth comes out through clues, nobody explains all of it):
The truth: Ostrin Vell's ledgers hold more than a dead clerk's sums. For a year a buyer who signs only as "S." has used Vell as a quiet broker. S. is Sorn Vathis, a factor for the Zhentarim. Through Vell he bought, at a discount, the loan notes of caravan masters on the Beregost–Nashkel stretch. Weeks later those same caravans vanished on the Way. The losses strengthen the Black Network's offer to guard the Trade Way for tolls, and the notes pay twice: once in profit, and once in debtors who must now sell cheap. Vell took his broker's fee and chose not to add it up. Jassan Ferr did add it up. He copied every S. entry in his own hand into a second ledger, locked it in the strongbox and sealed the box with an old Waukeenar stamp of his mother's instead of Vell's seal. Then his heart failed him, alone, three nights ago. Vell wants the box back unbroken because an unbroken seal is the only proof he can show Sorn that nobody has read it. He does not know the seal is not his, and he does not know about the copy. Nobody in Beregost holds the whole picture. Vell knows the brokering, Thale suspects the caravans, the Fist knows the losses, and only the box joins them.
Factions and their hidden aims:
- The Zhentarim (through the factor Sorn Vathis): To make the Beregost–Nashkel road look ungovernable, so the Council grants the Network the toll right, and to profit on the doomed caravans' debts along the way. Sorn wants every written trace of his buying gone or in his hands, unread. He means to collect the box from Vell at dusk, and he will ask whoever carried it what they saw.
- Thale's counting-room (Gerrit Thale, rival lender on the Trade Way): To ruin Vell and take his clients. Thale has heard Vell's debtors are dying on the road, and he wants the ledgers as leverage over Vell or as something to sell to the Fist. He has sent his man Coll Brannock to the cooper's yard to buy the box from the landlady, or to buy it from whoever carries it.
- The Flaming Fist garrison in Beregost: Short of men and money, and split. One sergeant wants proof of who profits from the vanished caravans and cannot pay for it. Others in the Fist quietly favour the Zhent toll offer because it would take the road off their hands. Proof handed to the wrong Fist officer goes nowhere.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Jassan Ferr kept a second ledger in his own hand: a copy of every entry for a client marked only "S.", with the dates, the debtors and the sums paid for their notes.
- Four of the caravans lost between Beregost and Nashkel this past year had loans from Vell. In each case the note was sold to "S." two to six weeks before the caravan vanished.
- Vell took a broker's fee on every one of those sales. He never asked why one buyer wanted only road debts.
- The seal on the strongbox is not Vell's. Jassan sealed the box himself with a lead stamp showing a pair of scales over a closed eye, an old mark of Waukeen's merchant bonds.
- Jassan owed the landlady, Wenna Pike, three gold and four silver in rent. She holds his key and has already sold his good coat to cover part of it.
- Gerrit Thale has told his man Coll Brannock he may pay up to a hundred gold for the box unopened, and more if it comes with Vell's own bearers to say where they got it.
- The day before he died, Jassan went to the Song of the Morning. He asked a priest whether a man is guilty for what he writes down for others. The priest remembers it.
- Jassan began a letter to the Fist sergeant in Beregost and never sent it. Half of it lies burnt in his room's grate, with the words "the notes were sold before" still legible.
- Sorn Vathis is in Beregost now, lodging at Feldepost's Inn under a cloth-merchant's name. He is waiting for dusk.
Clocks:
- clock_wenna_clears_room: Wenna Pike gives up on being paid and sells off the dead clerk's effects (segments 4; when full: She sells Jassan's things, the strongbox among them, to whoever pays the rent first. Coll Brannock is waiting to be that person.)
- clock_thale_moves: Coll Brannock works his way toward the box for Gerrit Thale (segments 6; when full: Coll and two hired men stop the company on the way back with Thale's offer: coin first, then a threat. He will take the box if it is left unwatched. He would rather not fight.)
- clock_sorn_arrives: Sorn Vathis comes to Vell's counting-house to collect what Jassan kept (segments 6; when full: At dusk Sorn is in Vell's back room. If the box is not there, or the seal is broken, Vell panics: he blames the hirelings to save himself, and Sorn starts asking about them.)
The wonder: The strongbox's seal: dark green wax over lead, stamped with a pair of scales above a closed eye. Under Light or a careful look the wax shows a faint inner grain, like a fingerprint that is not a fingerprint. The matching lead stamp lies wrapped in oilcloth under a loose floorboard in Jassan's room. Its history: Waukeenar temple-clerks of Baldur's Gate used it for "sealed-word" bonds before the goddess's disappearance in the Time of Troubles. A minor binding in the wax keeps the likeness of whoever breaks it, so a contract-holder could know who had read a sealed bond. Jassan's mother was such a clerk. After the old Waukeenar house in the Gate closed, she kept her stamp. The open question: These stamps were made in pairs, and a broken seal was meant to be shown to whoever held the twin. Jassan's stamp is the only one in the room. Who holds the other, and did Jassan choose this seal so that someone would know?
Clues to the truth:
- At the Song of the Morning, Brother Aldane remembers Jassan's question about guilt for what a man writes down for others. He also remembers that Jassan left a tithe in coin stamped from Zhentil Keep's old mint, which is unusual in Beregost.
- In the grate of Jassan's room lies a half-burnt draft addressed to "Sergeant Cowl of the Fist", with the words "the notes were sold before the wagons" still readable.
- In the Jovial Juggler's taproom, Harl Dobbin, a ruined caravan master, drinks on credit. His wagons and four guards were lost past the Lionsfang ford. Vell's note on him was sold, he says, to "some southern cloth man" a month before. He names the dead guards, and one may be a name Bram knows from th
The next session's false lead: On Jassan's nightstand there is a small dark vial with a bitter smell, and a stain on the floorboards beside it. It looks like poison. In truth it is foxglove tincture for a weak heart, prescribed by the Song of the Morning. He spilled it the night his heart gave out. Nobody killed Jassan Ferr; what he wrote down frightened him to death.
A character's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): Coll Brannock recognises Pell from the roofs of the Wide and uses the old name once, quietly, in front of whoever is there. He offers to forget it for an hour alone with the box, or for Pell's word that Thale gets first look. His source is that he ran with Wide crews in the Gate. It is a price on the table, not a trap, and Pell can read Coll's bluff better than anyone present.
The company's puzzles, threats and rewards (each with the player character it is first addressed to):
- puzzle, for Sefa Marrin: The scales-and-closed-eye seal: an old Waukeenar binding that keeps the face of whoever breaks it, and a twin stamp held by someone unknown.
- reward, for Sefa Marrin: Jassan's lead Waukeenar stamp, wrapped in oilcloth under the loose board — a minor magic item that seals "sealed-word" bonds and holds an open question.
- puzzle, for Pell Dunmore: Getting the box out of a room whose landlady holds the key and the rent, with a Guild-style chalk mark on the yard gate post saying the house is being watched.
- threat, for Pell Dunmore: Coll Brannock knows Pell's old Wide name and will spend that knowledge as a price.
- threat, for Bram Halloway: The letter's sender, who may come for Bram in person once between rounds 7 and 10, possibly within the others' hearing.
- reward, for Bram Halloway: Harl Dobbin at the Jovial Juggler, a ruined caravan master whose dead guards Bram may have known: the road's side of what the ledgers say.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): If Sefa turns her light on the seal, the Lantern lets her feel that she could see the twin stamp's holder, or read the ledger's first page through the wax, without breaking it. The sign is a warmth in her palms, and one line: "Only a little more owed." It speaks at the temptation to know, never to comfort.
The act plan (yours alone; the player sees only the act number): about 3 hours, ~30 turns; the errand: Bring Ostrin Vell the dead clerk Jassan Ferr's locked strongbox of ledgers from the room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way, unopened and with its seal whole, before nightfall, for 75 gold to share.
- act 1, to turn 4: The errand has been offered at Vell's counter (already done in the opening). The company may ask Vell questions, take the job, haggle or walk off, and reaches the Coast Way if they go. (converge: Any question to Vell, a stroll through Beregost, a visit to an inn or the temple passes through people who knew Jassan or saw Thale's man at the yard. Every road out of the counting-house runs along the Coast Way.)
- act 2, to turn 16: The room and its people: Wenna's rent, Tobin's account, the grate and the loose board, the seal itself. Coll Brannock turns up with his offer. At least one price, interest or secret conversation (Wenna, Coll or Brother Aldane). The world's chance of the letter's sender coming for Bram falls in round (converge: Whichever person a character pursues — the landlady, the cooper, the temple, the inn, Coll — each holds a piece that is about the box or bars its leaving. The box cannot leave the yard without someone paying, talking, sneaking or forcing.)
- act 3, to turn 24: The way back with the box. This is the fork where the three may disagree: pay Wenna or not, take Thale's offer or not, answer the letter or not, look at the seal by magic or leave it alone. Thale's men or the dusk deadline press on the road. (converge: Whatever the company decides about the box — deliver it, sell it, read it, hide it — the people who want it (Vell, Thale, Sorn) learn where it went and come to it.)
- act 4, to turn 30: The reckoning at dusk at Vell's, or wherever the box ends up. Sorn Vathis is present, the seal is shown whole or broken, and the ledger's meaning lands: the box was never about a clerk's sums. Payment, refusal or flight, each with its consequence. (converge: Every outcome — Vell paid, Thale paid, Fist told, box kept — leads to a meeting with the man who bought the road's debts. Who meets him, and on what terms, is the company's choice.)

Ostrin Vell: I want the box on my counter tonight, sealed, so I can say truthfully that no one read it. I brokered notes. Brokering is my trade; what buyers do afterwards is not my ledger. Jassan was careful. Too careful, maybe. I don't sit at his desk. I say what I mean in short sentences, and I don't say the name S. aloud.

Pell Dunmore: I work for coin, not favours. Favours are how the Guild kept me fifteen years. A locked box is a door like any other, and I know what doors cost. I don't use my old name and I don't want to hear it in this town. Three strangers hired together by a moneylender — I'm counting the exits.

Sefa Marrin: I left the hospice when the sisters stopped looking at my face. The Lantern answered me in the dark and I owe it something I've never been told the size of. I heal what I can reach. A man died alone in a room above a yard, and someone wants his box more than his body.

Coll Brannock: Mister Thale wants the box and he'll pay well for it, better than Vell. I'd rather buy than break heads; heads cost more. I ran with Wide crews in the Gate before I came south, and I remember faces off the roofs. I talk soft and friendly and leave the threat for the end of the sentence.

Gerrit Thale: Vell's debtors keep dying on the road and Vell keeps getting richer. I want to know why before the Fist does, or so I can tell them. I'm patient, I'm polite and I keep my books clean, which is more than he can say. If his hirelings want a better offer, my door is open, and so is my purse.

Tobin Aske: I make barrels. I heard him the last night through the boards, talking low, one voice, like praying, or arguing with himself. Then nothing. I found him in the morning. I don't want trouble in my yard and I don't want strangers on my stairs. Ask me plain and I'll answer plain. Ask me twice and I'll go back to my hoops.

Wenna Pike: Three gold and four silver, and he goes and dies owing it. Nobody leaves my house with a dead man's things until I'm paid. Not his master, not his friends, not the Fist. The quiet man from Thale's has been round twice with an open purse. I'm not cruel. I've got a roof to keep, and the dead don't pay rent.

fact.hidden_layer:
The campaign's hidden layer (the DM's prep; the player never sees it; the truth comes out through clues, nobody explains all of it):
The truth: Ostrin Vell's ledgers hold more than a dead clerk's sums. For a year a buyer who signs only as "S." has used Vell as a quiet broker. S. is Sorn Vathis, a factor for the Zhentarim. Through Vell he bought, at a discount, the loan notes of caravan masters on the Beregost–Nashkel stretch. Weeks later those same caravans vanished on the Way. The losses strengthen the Black Network's offer to guard the Trade Way for tolls, and the notes pay twice: once in profit, and once in debtors who must now sell cheap. Vell took his broker's fee and chose not to add it up. Jassan Ferr did add it up. He copied every S. entry in his own hand into a second ledger, locked it in the strongbox and sealed the box with an old Waukeenar stamp of his mother's instead of Vell's seal. Then his heart failed him, alone, three nights ago. Vell wants the box back unbroken because an unbroken seal is the only proof he can show Sorn that nobody has read it. He does not know the seal is not his, and he does not know about the copy. Nobody in Beregost holds the whole picture. Vell knows the brokering, Thale suspects the caravans, the Fist knows the losses, and only the box joins them.
Factions and their hidden aims:
- The Zhentarim (through the factor Sorn Vathis): To make the Beregost–Nashkel road look ungovernable, so the Council grants the Network the toll right, and to profit on the doomed caravans' debts along the way. Sorn wants every written trace of his buying gone or in his hands, unread. He means to collect the box from Vell at dusk, and he will ask whoever carried it what they saw.
- Thale's counting-room (Gerrit Thale, rival lender on the Trade Way): To ruin Vell and take his clients. Thale has heard Vell's debtors are dying on the road, and he wants the ledgers as leverage over Vell or as something to sell to the Fist. He has sent his man Coll Brannock to the cooper's yard to buy the box from the landlady, or to buy it from whoever carries it.
- The Flaming Fist garrison in Beregost: Short of men and money, and split. One sergeant wants proof of who profits from the vanished caravans and cannot pay for it. Others in the Fist quietly favour the Zhent toll offer because it would take the road off their hands. Proof handed to the wrong Fist officer goes nowhere.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Jassan Ferr kept a second ledger in his own hand: a copy of every entry for a client marked only "S.", with the dates, the debtors and the sums paid for their notes.
- Four of the caravans lost between Beregost and Nashkel this past year had loans from Vell. In each case the note was sold to "S." two to six weeks before the caravan vanished.
- Vell took a broker's fee on every one of those sales. He never asked why one buyer wanted only road debts.
- The seal on the strongbox is not Vell's. Jassan sealed the box himself with a lead stamp showing a pair of scales over a closed eye, an old mark of Waukeen's merchant bonds.
- Jassan owed the landlady, Wenna Pike, three gold and four silver in rent. She holds his key and has already sold his good coat to cover part of it.
- Gerrit Thale has told his man Coll Brannock he may pay up to a hundred gold for the box unopened, and more if it comes with Vell's own bearers to say where they got it.
- The day before he died, Jassan went to the Song of the Morning. He asked a priest whether a man is guilty for what he writes down for others. The priest remembers it.
- Jassan began a letter to the Fist sergeant in Beregost and never sent it. Half of it lies burnt in his room's grate, with the words "the notes were sold before" still legible.
- Sorn Vathis is in Beregost now, lodging at Feldepost's Inn under a cloth-merchant's name. He is waiting for dusk.
Clocks:
- clock_wenna_clears_room: Wenna Pike gives up on being paid and sells off the dead clerk's effects (segments 4; when full: She sells Jassan's things, the strongbox among them, to whoever pays the rent first. Coll Brannock is waiting to be that person.)
- clock_thale_moves: Coll Brannock works his way toward the box for Gerrit Thale (segments 6; when full: Coll and two hired men stop the company on the way back with Thale's offer: coin first, then a threat. He will take the box if it is left unwatched. He would rather not fight.)
- clock_sorn_arrives: Sorn Vathis comes to Vell's counting-house to collect what Jassan kept (segments 6; when full: At dusk Sorn is in Vell's back room. If the box is not there, or the seal is broken, Vell panics: he blames the hirelings to save himself, and Sorn starts asking about them.)
The wonder: The strongbox's seal: dark green wax over lead, stamped with a pair of scales above a closed eye. Under Light or a careful look the wax shows a faint inner grain, like a fingerprint that is not a fingerprint. The matching lead stamp lies wrapped in oilcloth under a loose floorboard in Jassan's room. Its history: Waukeenar temple-clerks of Baldur's Gate used it for "sealed-word" bonds before the goddess's disappearance in the Time of Troubles. A minor binding in the wax keeps the likeness of whoever breaks it, so a contract-holder could know who had read a sealed bond. Jassan's mother was such a clerk. After the old Waukeenar house in the Gate closed, she kept her stamp. The open question: These stamps were made in pairs, and a broken seal was meant to be shown to whoever held the twin. Jassan's stamp is the only one in the room. Who holds the other, and did Jassan choose this seal so that someone would know?
Clues to the truth:
- At the Song of the Morning, Brother Aldane remembers Jassan's question about guilt for what a man writes down for others. He also remembers that Jassan left a tithe in coin stamped from Zhentil Keep's old mint, which is unusual in Beregost.
- In the grate of Jassan's room lies a half-burnt draft addressed to "Sergeant Cowl of the Fist", with the words "the notes were sold before the wagons" still readable.
- In the Jovial Juggler's taproom, Harl Dobbin, a ruined caravan master, drinks on credit. His wagons and four guards were lost past the Lionsfang ford. Vell's note on him was sold, he says, to "some southern cloth man" a month before. He names the dead guards, and one may be a name Bram knows from th
The next session's false lead: On Jassan's nightstand there is a small dark vial with a bitter smell, and a stain on the floorboards beside it. It looks like poison. In truth it is foxglove tincture for a weak heart, prescribed by the Song of the Morning. He spilled it the night his heart gave out. Nobody killed Jassan Ferr; what he wrote down frightened him to death.
A character's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): Coll Brannock recognises Pell from the roofs of the Wide and uses the old name once, quietly, in front of whoever is there. He offers to forget it for an hour alone with the box, or for Pell's word that Thale gets first look. His source is that he ran with Wide crews in the Gate. It is a price on the table, not a trap, and Pell can read Coll's bluff better than anyone present.
The company's puzzles, threats and rewards (each with the player character it is first addressed to):
- puzzle, for Sefa Marrin: The scales-and-closed-eye seal: an old Waukeenar binding that keeps the face of whoever breaks it, and a twin stamp held by someone unknown.
- reward, for Sefa Marrin: Jassan's lead Waukeenar stamp, wrapped in oilcloth under the loose board — a minor magic item that seals "sealed-word" bonds and holds an open question.
- puzzle, for Pell Dunmore: Getting the box out of a room whose landlady holds the key and the rent, with a Guild-style chalk mark on the yard gate post saying the house is being watched.
- threat, for Pell Dunmore: Coll Brannock knows Pell's old Wide name and will spend that knowledge as a price.
- threat, for Bram Halloway: The letter's sender, who may come for Bram in person once between rounds 7 and 10, possibly within the others' hearing.
- reward, for Bram Halloway: Harl Dobbin at the Jovial Juggler, a ruined caravan master whose dead guards Bram may have known: the road's side of what the ledgers say.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): If Sefa turns her light on the seal, the Lantern lets her feel that she could see the twin stamp's holder, or read the ledger's first page through the wax, without breaking it. The sign is a warmth in her palms, and one line: "Only a little more owed." It speaks at the temptation to know, never to comfort.
The act plan (yours alone; the player sees only the act number): about 3 hours, ~30 turns; the errand: Bring Ostrin Vell the dead clerk Jassan Ferr's locked strongbox of ledgers from the room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way, unopened and with its seal whole, before nightfall, for 75 gold to share.
- act 1, to turn 4: The errand has been offered at Vell's counter (already done in the opening). The company may ask Vell questions, take the job, haggle or walk off, and reaches the Coast Way if they go. (converge: Any question to Vell, a stroll through Beregost, a visit to an inn or the temple passes through people who knew Jassan or saw Thale's man at the yard.
